documents: Published paper: Zhou & Zhou (2022), Tectonics 41, e2021TC007035 (PDF, 22 pages; supporting information not supplied)

entry.evidence: due to the lack of systematic analogue as well as numerical modeling experiments, the relationship between the structural vergence of thrust wedges

steps.action: Pose the problem that backward-vergent thrust wedges (e.g., Cascadia) are uncommon, reproduced only under specific model conditions, and not explained by 2D Coulomb wedge theory.
steps.quote: is difficult to be explained properly by the classic Coulomb wedge theory

steps.action: Take from published analogue models (Costa & Vendeville; Vendeville; Souloumiac et al.) the hypothesis that the lateral/basal shear stress ratio and the direction of lateral shear stress control vergence.
steps.quote: rather than the brittle overburden/basal shear strength ratio, might have controlled the structural vergence of thrust wedges

steps.action: Recall the authors' earlier sandbox models (Zhou et al., 2016): purely backward-vergent wedges form under backward-directed, high lateral shear stress and disappear when the sidewalls are removed.
steps.quote: purely backward-vergent thrust wedges may be formed under the condition of backward-directed

steps.action: Narrow the aim to two questions: the ratio-vergence relationship is not systematically known, and the origin of the ESXFTB is unresolved.
steps.quote: Its origin has confused the researchers of this region for many years and has not been proved by analogue or numerical models.

steps.action: Use a published seismic-reflection and surface-geology cross section showing a NW-vergent upper-crustal and a purely SE-vergent middle-crustal thrust system.
steps.quote: it comprises two oppositely vergent thrust systems at its upper and middle crusts

steps.action: State rival origins for the middle-crustal system: an earlier tectonic phase (Dong et al., 2015) versus the same single NW Mesozoic shortening.
steps.quote: some researchers argued that the middle crustal thrust system was produced from an earlier tectonic phase

steps.action: Derive that the earlier-phase rival predicts Mesozoic overprinting of the middle-crustal system, and compare this with the cross section, which shows none.
steps.quote: no evidence for such a deformation superimposition can be observed from the cross section

steps.action: Design two sandbox model types: Type A with one weak basal décollement for the general relationship, and Type B with two décollements for the ESXFTB. Vary the basal shear stress because sidewall friction cannot be changed.
steps.quote: Two types of sandbox models with one weak basal décollement (Type A models) and two weak décollements

steps.action: Characterize the analogue materials: sand internal and sidewall friction measured with a Hubbert-type shear box, and three silicone putties' viscosities measured with a Brookfield viscometer.
steps.quote: both of which were measured with a Hubbert-type shear box

steps.action: Set the lateral/basal ratio in the lab by changing shortening velocity, silicone viscosity and thickness: 14 ratios from 0.05 to 105.10 for Type A and 13 combinations for Type B, with representative runs selected.
steps.quote: Type A models were performed under fourteen different

steps.action: Check that both model types satisfy dynamic similarity with nature by computing model-to-nature ratios for cohesion and stress (Tables 3, 4).
steps.quote: suggesting that Type A models fulfill a dynamic similarity criterion

steps.action: Record the models by line-drawing and numbering thrusts in sidewall photographs, measuring thrust shortening, and deriving velocity and strain-rate fields with PIV software (MicroVec).
steps.quote: fields of the velocity and the strain rate of the models at different shortening stages were derived by MicroVec

steps.action: Check model artifacts: rear-part slumping did not change vergence; the Type B density inversion produced no diapirism; and sidewall views represent the whole model because there is no along-strike vergence change (Figure S1a).
steps.quote: This indicates that this phenomenon has not significantly affected the structural vergence of the models

steps.action: Repeat key models two to three times and report similar results (Figures S1b-S1d).
steps.quote: Key models of this study were repeated for two to three times to demonstrate the experimental reproducibility

steps.action: Describe the evolution of each run. Type A vergence goes frontward, then dual, then backward as the ratio increases, with wedge geometry and thrust shortening shares measured (Figure 5). In Type B the upper system goes frontward to dual to backward while the lower system stays purely backward.
steps.quote: clearly show progressive change in the structural vergence as well as the development of thrust wedges

steps.action: Fit ratio thresholds for one weak décollement (frontward <0.09, dual 0.09-1.15, backward >1.15; purely frontward <0.05, purely backward >105; preferred-vergence reversal between 0.15 and 0.17).
steps.quote: This demonstrates that τs/τd ratio is a key factor determining the structural vergence of thrust wedges

steps.action: Compare thresholds across Type A, Type B, Zhou et al. (2016) and Gutscher et al. (2001), estimating ratios for Gutscher's models from assumed parameters. Thresholds differ between model sets, and the progression is said to be compatible with Coulomb wedge theory.
steps.quote: Significant difference in structural vergence can also be observed between the models with different boundary conditions.

steps.action: Attribute the threshold differences to auxiliaries (adjacent thrust systems, boundary conditions, lateral shear stress direction, model width) rather than revising the ratio-control claim, and call for 3D mechanical analysis.
steps.quote: deformation in adjacent thrust systems at different levels, boundary conditions, and direction of lateral shear stress may influence the relationship

steps.action: Exclude the passive-roof duplex model for the ESXFTB: its vergence order is opposite, and it is confined to belt fronts.
steps.quote: the origin of the ESXFTB cannot be explained simply by the model of passive-roof duplex

steps.action: Compare Type B model ZC49 (lower ratio 15.86, upper ratio 0.34) with the ESXFTB cross section; it reproduces a purely backward-vergent lower system under a frontward-vergent upper system.
steps.quote: well reproduced a thrust wedge similar to the ESXFTB

steps.action: Retain the single NW Mesozoic shortening, acting on systems with different ratios, as the most likely origin of the ESXFTB; the two-event rival is judged not necessary.
steps.quote: they are most likely the results of the single northwestward Mesozoic shortening

end.claim: With one weak décollement, thrust wedge vergence changes progressively from frontward (ratio <0.09) to dual (0.09-1.15) to backward (>1.15) as the lateral/basal shear stress ratio increases, within the tested range 0.05-105.1.

decisive_move.sentence: Setting the lateral/basal shear stress ratio systematically across fourteen laboratory values, by varying shortening velocity, viscosity and silicone thickness, is what made the threshold regularity possible.

gates.evidence: The hypothesis that the ratio controls vergence (from prior models, p. 2) directed the choice to sweep the basal shear stress (p. 4). Vergence could have failed to change with the ratio, but the thresholds are read off the runs after the fact. The ESXFTB match is a single qualitative reproduction (p. 20). Nothing is stated as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Particle Image Velocimetry (MicroVec commercial software) for velocity and strain-rate fields
Dynamic similarity scaling via model-to-nature ratios
Commercial transparent silicone putty (Guangzhou Shisheng Chemical) as Newtonian analogue

novelty_claims.quote: Our model results revealed, for the first time, that structural vergence of thrust wedges lying on a weak décollement
the ESXFTB may be the first example of large purely backward-vergent thrust wedge accompanied by a frontward-vergent upper thrust system
neither analogue nor numerical models shortened from one end has successfully reproduced a structure similar to the ESXFTB
This work, however, has never been done in previous studies.

limits:
Sub-claims: the ESXFTB origin by single NW Mesozoic shortening is best_explanation (p. 20); the Type B result that oppositely vergent systems form simultaneously is a capability_characterized-style demonstration from three representative runs.

What is shown:
- Only 8 of 14 Type A and 3 of 13 Type B runs are reported in the main text; ZC33, ZC25 and ZC24 appear only in Figure 5 and the supplement. The selection criterion for representatives is not stated.
- Thresholds are read from discrete runs with no uncertainty bounds.
- The ratios are initial values computed from formulas, not measured during deformation.
- The repeat runs, along-strike views and some geometry data are in Supporting Information S1, which was not supplied, so the extent of reproduction cannot be checked.

Internal inconsistencies:
- ZC20 (ratio 0.09) is reported as frontward-vergent (p. 11), while the threshold is stated as dual for 0.09-1.15 (pp. 1, 17).
- The Figure 13b caption assigns ranges to backward- and dual-vergent wedges that differ from the text on p. 18.
- The Figure 14 caption names model ZC47 but panel b is ZC49.

Cross-study comparison: the Gutscher et al. (2001) ratios rest on assumed viscosity, friction and density.

Discordant thresholds: these are attributed to auxiliaries rather than tested (inference: protective move). Model width, decollement thickness, erosion and sedimentation were not varied.

Composition coded none_fits: a laboratory parameter sweep with conditions set, fitted as a regularity, is combined with a single analogue reproduction of one natural structure. Natures_repetition needs found conditions, and no single crucial test separates rivals as strong_inference requires.

No review file was supplied, though reviewers and the associate editor are acknowledged (p. 20); any review-forced changes are unknown.

disagreements.target: Classic 2D Coulomb wedge theory (Davis et al. 1983; Dahlen 1990)
disagreements.support: Lateral shear stress, absent in 2D theory, controls vergence in the models, although the vergence progression is called compatible with Coulomb theory predictions.
disagreements.quote: [...] the origin or dynamics of thrust wedges needs to be considered from a 3D perspective

disagreements.target: Brittle overburden/basal shear strength ratio as the control on vergence (Bonini 2001, 2003; Couzens-Schultz et al. 2003)
disagreements.support: Cited models with the same strength ratio but different lateral/basal ratios show different vergences.
disagreements.quote: rather than the brittle overburden/basal shear strength ratio, might have controlled the structural vergence of thrust wedges

disagreements.target: Dong et al. (2015): middle crustal thrust system from an earlier Paleoproterozoic Yangtze-Cathaysia collision
disagreements.support: There is no superimposition evidence in the cross section, and model ZC49 reproduces both systems in one shortening.
disagreements.quote: are not necessarily the products of two opposite shortening events

disagreements.target: Passive-roof duplex model as explanation of the ESXFTB (Banks & Warburton 1986; Couzens-Schultz et al. 2003)
